title: Documentation
text: MarkdownUtil is a .NET 10 tool for writing documentation in ordinary Markdown and publishing it as a static HTML site. It brings linting, local preview, and rendering into one CLI, while the folder structure supplies the site navigation.

title: Documentation
text: Use one .NET tool for the docs workflow. Lint pages, preview changes, and render the site without a separate Node.js or Python build toolchain. Turn folders into a navigable site. MarkdownUtil builds the sidebar and breadcrumbs from README.md pages and their folder structure. Find link issues before publishing. The linter checks local links, images, and path casing, and reports the source file and line. Keep your Markdown and choose your host. The sources remain readable Markdown, and the rendered output is static HTML. Optional sidebar.order metadata is specific to MarkdownUtil.

title: Features
text: Code Blocks - Displays fenced code blocks with syntax highlighting Sidebar - Describes the generated sidebar and how to control its order Tables - Examples of rendered Markdown tables Diagrams - Renders Mermaid flowcharts and sequence diagrams, PlantUML component diagrams, and context diagrams to static SVG that follows the light and dark theme Admonitions - Highlights notes, tips, and warnings with GitHub-compatible alert syntax Breadcrumb navigation is generated from the Markdown file structure during rendering; source files remain unchanged.

title: Setup
text: MarkdownUtil is distributed as a .NET tool through NuGet . It requires .NET 10.

title: Setup
text: Install the .NET 10 runtime for your operating system.

title: Setup
text: Install the tool globally for your system or locally for a repository.

title: Setup
text: dotnet tool install --global MarkdownUtil

title: Setup
text: A local tool is available in the repository and its subfolders. A local tool requires a tool manifest. dotnet new tool-manifest # if you are setting up this repo for the first time dotnet tool install --local MarkdownUtil

title: Usage
text: Run commands from the project folder. Commands that read Markdown use ./docs or ./Docs by default. render and serve write the generated site to ./site . For a project with a Docs directory: mdu lint mdu render mdu serve mdu lint reads the Markdown files and reports any problems. mdu render writes the static site to ./site and exits. mdu serve renders the site to ./site , opens it in your browser, and watches Markdown files and linked local assets for changes. Press Ctrl+C to stop the preview server. Both render and serve generate breadcrumb navigation in the HTML from the Markdown file structure. The Markdown files are left unchanged. For example, a missing local link is reported with its file and line: /project/Docs/Overview.md:7: MDU004 LocalLinkExists: Local link target './intro.md' does not exist. Linter detected 1 error. You can specify the source directory, output directory, and port when needed. The preview defaults to ./site and port 4173 . mdu render mdu serve --port 4173 Use --no-browser to start the server without opening a browser.

title: Usage
text: Command Purpose Details mdu lint [path] Checks Markdown pages and local links. Alias: mdu l . lint mdu render [path] [outpath] Writes a static HTML site. Alias: mdu r . render mdu serve [path] [outpath] Serves a local preview and updates it when files change. serve mdu tree [path] Prints the detected Markdown page structure. Alias: mdu print . tree For path , MarkdownUtil uses the only ./docs or ./Docs directory in the current folder when one exists. If neither exists, or both exist, pass the path explicitly. render and serve use ./site as the default outpath . All four commands search for *.md files by default; use --pattern (or -p ) to choose another file pattern.

title: Architecture
text: This section describes how MarkdownUtil turns Markdown source into a rendered site. HTML Renderer - Describes the generated pages and how they are rendered

title: Other Tools
text: Static site generators for Markdown documentation are not new, and many good solutions already exist. Please note: This project was created to follow the principle of "eating our own dog food" and should be understood in that context. This tool is tailored to the author's current needs and may introduce breaking changes at any time. This policy will remain in place until the project reaches an appropriate level of production readiness. Check out the other tools if you are looking for an established project with a much larger community.

title: Other Tools
text: This is a short list of interesting free alternatives from the author's perspective. It is not intended to be comprehensive. Docusaurus - Free documentation platform built with React by Meta, with source code on GitHub . MkDocs - Free Python-based documentation generator, with source code on GitHub . VuePress - Free Vue-powered static site generator, with source code on GitHub .

title: Sidebar
text: When you run mdu serve , MarkdownUtil creates a collapsible sidebar from the Markdown files in the documentation folder. A README.md represents its folder in the navigation, and child folders appear nested below it. The root documentation page stays expanded; nested pages with child pages have a disclosure button to expand or collapse them. Selecting a nested page with child pages expands its section automatically. The current page stays highlighted in gray until hovered, when it uses the hover color. Expanded sections stay open while you navigate during the current session. By default, entries at the same level are sorted alphabetically by page title. Add a sidebar.order number to a page's YAML front matter to choose its position. Smaller numbers appear first. Pages with an order are listed before pages without one; unordered pages remain alphabetical. If two pages have the same order, they are sorted alphabetically by title.

title: Sidebar
text: Put the sidebar field at the top of the Markdown file, before its title. For example, this front matter in Docs/Setup/README.md places Setup before the other top-level sections: --- sidebar: order: 10 --- The MarkdownUtil documentation uses this ordering for its top-level sections: Page sidebar.order Docs/Setup/README.md 10 Docs/Usage/README.md 20 Docs/Features/README.md 30 Docs/Architecture/README.md 35 Docs/OtherTools/README.md 40 For a single setting, you can also use the compact form: --- sidebar.order: 10 --- MarkdownUtil recognizes sidebar.order as a compact alternative to the nested form. If both sidebar: { order: ... } and sidebar.order: ... are present, the nested form takes precedence. The numbers only order siblings at the same level. For example, the value in Docs/Features/README.md positions the Features section among the other top-level sections. Values in files beneath Docs/Features/ control their positions inside that section.

title: Sidebar
text: Set sidebar.visible to false to omit a page from the sidebar. Pages are visible by default. If the page represents a folder, its child pages remain visible at the next higher level: --- sidebar: visible: false ---

title: Admonitions
text: Admonitions, also called alerts or callouts, highlight information that readers should not miss. MarkdownUtil uses the same syntax as GitHub alerts , so your files look right on GitHub and in the rendered site.

title: Admonitions
text: Start a block quote with the alert type on its own line, then write the content on the following lines: > [!NOTE] > Useful information that users should know, even when skimming content. MarkdownUtil supports all five GitHub alert types: > [!NOTE] > Useful information that users should know, even when skimming content. > [!TIP] > Helpful advice for doing things better or more easily. > [!IMPORTANT] > Key information users need to know to achieve their goal. > [!WARNING] > Urgent info that needs immediate user attention to avoid problems. > [!CAUTION] > Advises about risks or negative outcomes of certain actions.

title: Admonitions
text: The examples below are rendered from the Markdown above. Use the theme switch in the header to see them in light and dark mode. Note Useful information that users should know, even when skimming content. Tip Helpful advice for doing things better or more easily. Important Key information users need to know to achieve their goal. Warning Urgent info that needs immediate user attention to avoid problems. Caution Advises about risks or negative outcomes of certain actions. An admonition can contain any Markdown, such as several paragraphs, lists, links, and code: Tip Preview your documentation while you write: mdu serve The Usage section describes all commands.

title: Admonitions
text: MarkdownUtil follows the same rules as GitHub: The marker must be the first line of a block quote and stand alone on that line. Text after the marker, such as > [!NOTE] Text , renders a regular block quote. The type is not case-sensitive: [!NOTE] , [!Note] , and [!note] are equivalent. Only NOTE , TIP , IMPORTANT , WARNING , and CAUTION are alert types. Any other type renders a regular block quote. The marker must be followed by content. A block quote that contains only the marker remains a regular block quote. Admonitions cannot be nested inside lists or other block quotes.

title: Admonitions
text: MarkdownUtil uses Markdig's alert blocks and renders the same HTML structure as GitHub: a div with the classes markdown-alert and markdown-alert-<type> , for example markdown-alert-tip , followed by a markdown-alert-title paragraph. The title is shown without an icon, and the colors adapt to the light and dark themes.

title: Code Blocks
text: Fenced code blocks display code or commands without interpreting their contents as Markdown. Add a language identifier after the opening fence to enable syntax highlighting.

title: Code Blocks
text: Add a language identifier after the opening backticks: ```csharp var greeting = "Hello, world!"; Console.WriteLine(greeting); ``` The rendered result keeps the code in a scrollable block and highlights supported syntax: var greeting = "Hello, world!"; Console.WriteLine(greeting); If you omit the language identifier or use an unsupported one, the code is rendered without syntax highlighting: This is plain code.

title: Code Blocks
text: Use one of these language identifiers: Language Identifiers C# cs , csharp Swift swift YAML yaml , yml Shell bash , zsh , sh , shell The highlighter uses lightweight language rules rather than full language parsers, so it colors selected syntax elements. Other languages remain readable as plain code.

title: tree
text: mdu tree prints the titles of the detected Markdown pages as an indented tree. A folder's README.md acts as its parent page; pages in child folders are shown beneath it.

title: tree
text: mdu tree PATH --pattern PATTERN The alias mdu print also runs this command. For all arguments, options, and defaults, here is the output of mdu tree --help : Description: Prints the detected Markdown files as a tree. Usage: mdu tree [<path>] [options] Arguments: <path> Root folder containing Markdown files. Defaults to ./docs or ./Docs. Options: -p, --pattern <pattern> Search pattern for Markdown files. [default: *.md] --hidden Include hidden files and folders. -?, -h, --help Show help and usage information

title: tree
text: Print the default documentation tree or choose a folder explicitly: mdu tree mdu tree ./ProjectDocs Use a different file pattern when pages use another extension: mdu tree ./ProjectDocs --pattern "*.markdown" Back to Usage

title: lint
text: mdu lint checks Markdown files under a root folder and reports rule violations with the source file and line number. It exits with code 1 when it finds errors and 0 when it does not.

title: lint
text: mdu lint PATH --pattern PATTERN The alias mdu l runs the same command. For all arguments, options, and defaults, here is the output of mdu lint --help : Description: Runs the linter and prints the results. Usage: mdu lint [<path>] [options] Arguments: <path> Root folder containing Markdown files. Defaults to ./docs or ./Docs. Options: -p, --pattern <pattern> Search pattern for Markdown files. [default: *.md] --hidden Include hidden files and folders. -?, -h, --help Show help and usage information

title: lint
text: Rule 1 - Every Markdown page must have a level-one heading that defines its title (after any YAML front matter). Rule 2 - Directory names must match the title in the index file ( README.md ). Rule 3 - The casing of internal links in a Markdown file must match the casing of their targets. Rule 4 - Local links and image targets must point to an existing file or to a directory with a README.md index. Each diagnostic includes a stable code, a descriptive rule name, the source path, and the line number. For example, MDU004 is named LocalLinkExists : /project/Docs/Overview.md:7: MDU004 LocalLinkExists: Local link target './intro.md' does not exist. The linter also lists completely orphaned pages: pages hidden from the sidebar with sidebar.visible: false that no visible page links to. This list is informational and does not affect the lint exit code.

title: lint
text: Check the default documentation folder: mdu lint Check a specific folder or only files matching a different pattern: mdu lint ./ProjectDocs mdu lint ./ProjectDocs --pattern "*.markdown" An error includes the path, line, rule code, and message. For example: /project/Docs/Overview.md:7: MDU004 LocalLinkExists: Local link target './intro.md' does not exist. Back to Usage

title: render
text: mdu render converts the detected Markdown pages into a static HTML site. It writes the result and copied local assets to the output folder, which defaults to ./site . The command exits after rendering.

title: render
text: mdu render PATH OUTPATH --pattern PATTERN --editPageRoot URL The alias mdu r runs the same command. For all arguments, options, and defaults, here is the output of mdu render --help : Description: Renders Markdown files to a static HTML site. Usage: mdu render [<path> [<outpath>]] [options] Arguments: <path> Root folder containing Markdown files. Defaults to ./docs or ./Docs. <outpath> Output folder for rendered files. Defaults to ./site. Options: -p, --pattern <pattern> Search pattern for Markdown files. [default: *.md] --hidden Include hidden files and folders. --editPageRoot <editPageRoot> URL to the root URL for editing the source files. -?, -h, --help Show help and usage information --editPageRoot adds an Edit Page link to each rendered page.

title: render
text: Render the default documentation folder to ./site , or choose both folders explicitly: mdu render mdu render ./ProjectDocs ./public/docs Render only files matching a pattern and add links to their source files in a GitHub repository: mdu render ./Docs ./site --pattern "*.md" --editPageRoot "https://github.com/example/project/edit/main/Docs" The Markdown source files are left unchanged. Back to Usage

title: serve
text: mdu serve renders the Markdown site, starts a local preview server, and watches the source folder for changes. Markdown pages and linked local assets are updated as you work. By default, the command opens the preview in a browser and listens on port 4173 . Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

title: serve
text: mdu serve PATH OUTPATH --pattern PATTERN --port PORT --no-browser --editPageRoot URL For all arguments, options, and defaults, here is the output of mdu serve --help : Description: Renders, serves, and watches a Markdown site. Usage: mdu serve [<path> [<outpath>]] [options] Arguments: <path> Root folder containing the Markdown files. Defaults to ./docs or ./Docs. <outpath> Output folder for the rendered site. Defaults to ./site. Options: -p, --pattern <pattern> Search pattern for Markdown files. [default: *.md] --hidden Include hidden files and folders. --port <port> Local preview server port. [default: 4173] --no-browser Do not open the preview in a browser. --editPageRoot <editPageRoot> URL to the root URL for editing the source files. -?, -h, --help Show help and usage information

title: serve
text: Start the default preview, or serve a specific documentation folder on another port: mdu serve mdu serve ./ProjectDocs ./site --port 8080 Run the preview without opening a browser: mdu serve --no-browser Back to Usage

title: Rule 3
text: The casing of internal links must match the casing of their targets on the local file system.

title: Rule 3
text: When documentation is edited on a case-insensitive file system (such as the default file system on Windows), an incorrectly cased internal link may go unnoticed and later fail on a case-sensitive deployment.

title: Rule 3
text: For example, you might link to the parent page that contains an overview: Click [here](../README.md) to return to the overview page. If the parent file is actually named readme.md , the link may still work on a Windows machine but be broken on Linux, where file name casing matters.

title: Rule 2
text: The name of a directory containing a README.md file must match the title in that file.

title: Rule 2
text: README.md files act as index files that readers open when they enter a directory, so they typically contain the most important information about it. However, their titles may not indicate what the directory contains. When the directory name matches the README title, readers can tell what the index covers while navigating the project. For example, if a README.md file is in a docs directory, its title should be Docs .

title: Rule 2
text: Assume a README.md file with the following content: # notes These are my notes. It is good practice to name the directory notes as well.

title: Rule 2
text: Titles such as "Rule 2: This is a following description" are truncated at the colon to avoid long directory names.

title: HTML Renderer
text: Light and dark themes, with an automatic mode that follows the operating system. A collapsible, responsive sitemap navigation. Responsive, mobile-first layouts. Syntax highlighting for code blocks. GitHub-compatible admonitions for notes, tips, and warnings. Client-side search with direct links to matching sections and highlighted occurrences. Automatic copying of assets to the output directory. Breadcrumb navigation generated from the Markdown file structure.

title: HTML Renderer
text: The embedded HTML template is rendered by HtmlRenderer using .NET string and HTML-encoding APIs; it has no separate template engine dependency. Markdig renders Markdown (CommonMark) files as HTML. Search creates a static JSON index at render time; the browser searches it locally without a search service.

title: Diagrams
text: MarkdownUtil draws diagrams from fenced code blocks while it renders your Markdown. It understands a subset of the Mermaid and PlantUML syntax and turns each diagram into static SVG that is embedded directly in the generated HTML page. Important MarkdownUtil does not contain Mermaid or PlantUML, and it does not call them. It only imitates part of their syntax and draws the diagrams with its own implementation. The result therefore looks different from the originals, and not every feature is available.

title: Diagrams
text: Mermaid and PlantUML are fantastic projects, and I have enormous respect for the people who build and maintain them. Many documentation sites would not be what they are without them. MarkdownUtil follows one firm architectural rule: .NET and NuGet packages are its only dependencies. Mermaid renders in the browser with JavaScript, and PlantUML needs a Java runtime. Bundling either of them would break that rule, so I decided to implement the diagrams myself instead of depending on these projects. Drawing the diagrams myself also has big advantages for me. Because every shape, line, and label comes from MarkdownUtil's own code, it is extremely easy to give the diagrams exactly the look and feel of the rest of the page: the same fonts, colors, and light and dark themes, without fighting another tool's styling.

title: Diagrams
text: Every diagram is finished when mdu render or mdu serve writes the page: The page contains plain SVG. No JavaScript runs in the browser, and no diagram service is contacted. Diagrams appear immediately and also work offline. The colors come from the page's stylesheet, so diagrams follow the light and dark theme automatically.

title: Diagrams
text: Your diagrams stay in the standard notation, so you can leave MarkdownUtil at any time without rewriting them: Mermaid diagrams stay ordinary ```mermaid code blocks. GitHub and other Mermaid-aware tools render the same files with the real Mermaid. PlantUML diagrams stay ordinary ```plantuml code blocks that PlantUML itself and PlantUML-aware tools render. Context diagrams are the exception: they are a MarkdownUtil extension in ```context code blocks, which other tools show as plain code. If a diagram uses syntax outside the supported subset, such as subgraph or other diagram types, MarkdownUtil shows its source as a code block instead of guessing.

title: Diagrams
text: ```mermaid flowchart TD Start([Open a Markdown file]) --> Lint{Lint passes?} Lint -->|Yes| Render[Render HTML] Lint -->|No| Fix[Fix the reported issues] Fix --> Lint Render --> Publish((Publish)) ``` flowchart TD Start([Open a Markdown file]) --> Lint{Lint passes?} Lint -->|Yes| Render[Render HTML] Lint -->|No| Fix[Fix the reported issues] Fix --> Lint Render --> Publish((Publish)) Use LR for a diagram that flows from left to right: flowchart LR Docs[Docs folder] --> Render[mdu render] --> Site[Static site] Render -.-> Search[Search index]

title: Diagrams
text: MarkdownUtil follows PlantUML's component diagram syntax, so the same source works with PlantUML itself: Element Syntax Frame @startuml and @enduml are optional Components [Name] , [Name] as Alias , component Name , component "Name" as Alias , component Alias as "Name" Interfaces () "Name" , () "Name" as Alias , interface Name ; an unknown name in a link also becomes an interface Other elements actor , database , node , cloud , folder , frame , package , rectangle , card , artifact , file , queue , storage Containers Any of package , node , folder , frame , cloud , database , rectangle , or component followed by { … } , also nested and without a name Stereotypes <<name>> after the element Links -- solid, .. dotted, == bold, with > or < for arrow ends, for example --> or <.. ; triangle ends are described below Link direction -> keeps both elements in one row, --> puts the target below, more dashes make the link longer; -up-> , -down-> , -left-> , -right-> (also -u-> and so on) Link styles -[hidden]-> only affects the layout, -[dashed]-> , -[bold]-> Link labels A --> B : Text Notes note left of A : Text , note right of , note top of , note bottom of , multi-line notes ending with end note , note "Text" as N Layout left to right direction , top to bottom direction Text title Text , \n for a line break Comments Lines starting with ' and /' … '/ blocks A triangle end, as for realization or generalization, is written ..|> or <|-- . skinparam , hide , show , and colors are ignored, because the page theme defines the look. Other PlantUML diagram types, such as sequence or class diagrams, stay code blocks.

title: Diagrams
text:
A context diagram shows one system in the center and the people and systems it works with around it. Note Context diagrams are a MarkdownUtil extension. Neither Mermaid nor PlantUML has this diagram type, so only mdu renders them. GitHub and other tools show the ```context block as plain code. A context diagram uses the flowchart syntax for systems and links, and actor for people: ```context MC[Mobile Capture] MC <--> IdP[Zuvex
IdP] MC <--> DRiVe[DRiVe

E-Mail Server] MC --> AD[Active
Directory] actor LK as Lehrkräfte actor SL as Schulleitung LK -. Verwendet .-> MC SL -.-> MC ``` MC[Mobile Capture] MC <--> IdP[Zuvex
IdP] MC <--> DRiVe[DRiVe
Verfahren] MC --> DB[Datenbank] MC --> Mail[Dataport

title: Diagrams
text: Element Syntax Systems The flowchart shapes, for example A[Text] , A(Text) , A([Text]) , A((Text)) , A{Text} People actor A or actor A as Label Links The flowchart links, link ends, and labels, for example --> , <--> , -.-> , ==> , and A -- Text --> B Titles accTitle: Text Comments Lines starting with %% The system in the center is the one that every link connects to. If several systems qualify, for example with a single link, the first one in the source is used. All other systems and people are spread evenly around the center, clockwise from the top in the order they first appear, so you control the arrangement by reordering the lines. A context diagram needs no header line.
